body_html:
Spanish accent marks look like decoration to many learners, so they get skipped. But a written accent (tilde) does real work: it shows which syllable is stressed and sometimes separates two different words, like si (if) and sí (yes). The rules are surprisingly logical, and once you learn three stress patterns you can predict almost every accent in the language.

Key takeaways
  • Spanish has one written accent mark: the acute accent (á, é, í, ó, ú).
  • Words ending in a vowel, n or s are stressed on the second-to-last syllable; others on the last. Accents mark exceptions.
  • Words stressed on the third-to-last syllable always carry an accent: música, teléfono.
  • Question words take accents: qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo.
{{toc}}

Spanish accent marks: the three stress rules

TypeStressAccent mark?Examples
agudaslast syllableOnly if the word ends in a vowel, n or scafé, canción, después / hablar, reloj
llanassecond-to-lastOnly if it does not end in a vowel, n or sárbol, fácil, lápiz / casa, examen
esdrújulasthird-to-lastAlwaysmúsica, sábado, teléfono

In short: the default stress is predictable, and the accent appears only when a word breaks the default. The RAE’s Diccionario panhispánico de dudas sets out these rules officially.

Accents that change meaning

Some short words carry an accent only to tell them apart from an identical word (the tilde diacrítica):

No accentWith accent
si ifsí yes
tu yourtú you
el theél he
mi mymí me (after prepositions)
te you (object)té tea
se himself, etc.sé I know
de ofdé give (subjunctive)
mas but (literary)más more

And in longer words, moving the stress changes the word: papa (potato) vs papá (dad), esta (this) vs está (is), hablo (I speak) vs habló (he spoke). That last pair shows why accents matter in verbs: they mark tense. These pairs are also collected in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|Spanish confusing words}}.

{{image:2}}

Question and exclamation words

Qué, quién, cuál, cómo, dónde, cuándo, cuánto take an accent in direct and indirect questions and exclamations:

  • ¿Dónde vives? Where do you live?
  • No sé cuándo llega. I don’t know when she arrives.
  • ¡Qué bonito! How beautiful!

Without a question or exclamation, no accent: Vivo donde vive mi familia. / Creo que sí. The same goes for porque (because) vs por qué (why).

When accents appear and disappear

Adding a syllable can shift a word into a different stress category:

  • canción → canciones (accent disappears)
  • examen → exámenes (accent appears)
  • joven → jóvenes
  • dime → dímelo, compra → cómpralo (pronouns added)
{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Ñ is not an accent

The ñ is a separate letter, not an n with an accent, and forgetting it can change the word completely. The classic example: año means year, but without the tilde it becomes a word for a part of the body you would not put in a birthday card. Always write Feliz año nuevo and Tengo 30 años with the ñ.

Capital letters keep their accents

A common myth says capitals don’t need accents. The RAE is clear that they do: ÁFRICA, Álvaro, Él llegó tarde.

How to type Spanish accents

  • Phone: press and hold the vowel or n and choose the accented letter.
  • Mac: Option + E, then the vowel (á); Option + N, then N (ñ).
  • Windows: add the “Spanish” or “US International” keyboard; with US International, type ' then the vowel.
  • ¿ and ¡: on a Mac, Option + Shift + ? and Option + 1.

Accents matter in messages too; see {{link:texting-in-spanish|texting in Spanish}} for what natives skip and what they don’t.

Do native speakers skip accents?

In quick text messages, yes, many native speakers drop accents, and nobody minds. In emails, school work, job applications and anything published, missing accents look careless, much like writing “its” for “it’s” in English. As a translator, I treat accents as non-negotiable in professional work. My advice for learners: write them from day one, because it trains you to notice stress when you speak. Reading carefully edited Spanish, such as bilingual books, also builds an instinct for where accents belong, so that a word like cancion without its accent starts to look wrong to you.

Try it yourself

Add the accents where needed: musica, arbol, cafe, joven, jovenes, telefono, examen, ¿como estas?

Answers: música, árbol, café, joven, jóvenes, teléfono, examen, ¿cómo estás? If you got joven and examen right without accents, you’ve understood the rules.

Accents are one of the writing mistakes in {{link:common-spanish-mistakes|my guide to common Spanish mistakes}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Spanish accent marks follow rules, not whims. Learn the three stress patterns, the short diacritical pairs and the question words, and you’ll get nearly every accent right. And never forget the ñ in año.

faq.q: When do Spanish words need an accent mark?
faq.a: When the stress breaks the default pattern: last-syllable stress on words ending in a vowel, n or s (canción), second-to-last stress on words ending in other consonants (árbol), and always on third-to-last stress (música).

faq.q: Do capital letters need accents in Spanish?
faq.a: Yes. The RAE requires accents on capital letters: Álvaro, ÁFRICA.
No. Ñ is a separate letter of the Spanish alphabet, and año (year) and ano are different words.
